concepts.title: Correlation and Regression in Biological Data
concepts.definition: When two variables such as heart rate and systolic pressure are measured across ten patients, an eyeball check cannot certify their association; regression draws the best-fit line and reports an R-squared between zero and one that measures how tightly points hug it, while correlation only quantifies the connectedness - and a good fit lets the null hypothesis be rejected.
concepts.key_idea: Average each variable first, then let the regression line and its R-squared decide whether the variables truly move together.

concepts.title: Statistical Significance and the P-value
concepts.definition: A p-value gives the chance of seeing the observed result if the null hypothesis were true, and a cutoff of 0.05 - that is, ninety-five percent significance - has been the traditional pass mark, although the chapter warns that this threshold breeds false positives and small samples are better shown as all data points rather than averages with standard deviations.
concepts.key_idea: Subtract the cutoff from one and multiply by a hundred to convert it into a significance percentage.
question_patterns: convert the conventional p-value cutoff of 0.05 into a percent significance level

solution_steps.explain: Significance equals one minus the cutoff probability.
Multiply by one hundred to express it as a percentage.

concepts.title: Scope and Milestones of Bioinformatics
concepts.definition: Bioinformatics fuses biology with computer science, mathematics, statistics and engineering to store, retrieve and interpret molecular data; Margaret Dayhoff's 1965 Atlas of Protein Sequence pioneered it, GenBank opened in 1982, the word itself entered literature around 1991, and the human genome project pushed it into the mainstream of genome-wide analysis.
concepts.key_idea: Sequence databases and the genome era turned a quiet support craft into a discipline every biologist now needs.
question_patterns: define bioinformatics and name the disciplines that meet at its intersection
which 1965 publication by Margaret Dayhoff became the model for sequence databases
in which year was GenBank launched and what does it store
when did the term bioinformatics begin appearing in the literature
why did structural bioinformatics precede genome-wide informatics
how do data mining and hypothesis generation fit the goals of bioinformatics

solution_steps.explain: 1965 Atlas, 1982 GenBank, 1991 first literature use, then the human genome project boom.
High-throughput sequencers and microarrays feed the pipelines that statistics and algorithms digest.
Stored, annotated and interpreted data that generate biological insight and new hypotheses.

worked_examples.q: Whose 1965 Atlas of Protein Sequence pioneered bioinformatics: Margaret Dayhoff's or Mendel's?

concepts.title: Biological Databases and Data Portals
concepts.definition: A biological database is a machine-searchable library of organised biological information, run by a database management system through query languages for relational designs or NoSQL schemes for scattered unstructured data; the workhorses are GenBank for DNA sequences, PDB for 3D structures, UniProt for proteins, PubMed for literature, KEGG for pathways and OMIM for human genes and disorders.
concepts.key_idea: Match the data type to its portal - sequences, structures, pathways or literature - and judge a database by access, documentation and upkeep.
question_patterns: match GenBank PDB UniProt PubMed KEGG and OMIM with the data type each archives
differentiate relational from non-relational databases with reference to SQL
what makes a biological database a good one - list four desirable characteristics

which database would you search for a 3D structure of a protein complex
what does the database management system of a repository do

solution_steps.explain: Sequence, structure, pathway, literature or disease catalog decides the portal.
Relational stores use structured query language; NoSQL serves large unstructured collections.
Ease of access, documentation, cross-references and continuous updating mark a reliable repository.

worked_examples.q: Which database stores 3D structures: PDB or PubMed?

concepts.title: Experimental Technologies for Biomolecule Analysis
concepts.definition: Each biomolecule has its profiling tools: PCR amplifies DNA, real-time qPCR reads RNA expression, next-generation sequencers read genes and transcriptomes, gel electrophoresis sorts DNA, RNA and proteins by size and charge, HPLC separates metabolites, mass spectrometry fragments molecules to weigh them, and electron microscopy resolves structure and sequence.
concepts.key_idea: Pick the technology by the molecule and the question - amplification, expression, sequence, separation, mass or structure.
question_patterns: match PCR qPCR next-generation sequencing gel electrophoresis HPLC and mass spectrometry with the biomolecule each assays

solution_steps.explain: DNA, RNA, protein or metabolite decides the toolset.
Amplify, detect expression, sequence, separate, weigh or visualise.
Each technology outputs a characteristic data type - reads, intensity files, chromatograms or mass spectra.

worked_examples.q: Which technology amplifies DNA: PCR or HPLC?

concepts.title: FASTA and FASTQ Record Arithmetic
concepts.definition: Sequences travel as text: a FASTA record opens with a greater-than description line followed by single-letter sequence, while FASTQ spends four lines per read - an at-sign header, the raw letters, a plus line and an equal-length quality line whose exclamation and tilde marks bracket the quality scale - so counting lines and letters sizes any file.
concepts.key_idea: Four lines hide in every FASTQ record, and the quality string must match the sequence letter for letter.
question_patterns: a FASTQ file holds 4000 lines - how many reads does it store

why do quality scores accompany high-throughput sequencing reads

solution_steps.explain: Every read occupies exactly four lines in FASTQ.
Multiply the reads by the read length.

worked_examples.q: How many lines does one FASTQ record hold?

concepts.title: Sequencing Reads and Coverage Arithmetic
concepts.definition: High-throughput instruments emit short reads of roughly 100-150 nucleotides or long reads of a few kilobases; covering a genome therefore needs the genome size divided by the read length, and sequencing centres - the Broad Institute alone passes twenty-four terabytes a day - split such workloads into runs of fixed read capacity.
concepts.key_idea: Divide the genome by the read length for the read count, then by reads per run for the number of runs.
question_patterns: how many reads of 150 nucleotides are needed to cover a 3 billion base genome once
a genome centre produces 24 terabytes of genome data per day - how much does it produce in a week

solution_steps.explain: Each read tiles that many bases of the genome.
Divide the reads by the per-run capacity.

concepts.title: Genome Informatics Workflow and Artificial Intelligence
concepts.definition: After quality control, reads either align to a reference or assemble de novo into contigs; the finished genome then gets annotated for genes and repeats, scanned by gene predictors, described through gene ontology terms, and placed in phylogenetic trees with tools like PHYLIP, while machine learning - already calling genomic variants and reading eye images - promises the next leap if multidisciplinary teams keep pace with the data flood.
concepts.key_idea: Quality-check, assemble or align, annotate, predict, and finally interpret - with AI joining the pipeline at every step.
question_patterns: name the two modalities of analysis that follow sequencing

which three aspects of gene products does gene ontology describe
what does a phylogenetic tree convey and which tools compute evolutionary distances
how are machine learning algorithms already used on genomic variants
why does successful AI in bioinformatics demand multidisciplinary collaboration

solution_steps.explain: Quality control and adaptor trimming precede every workflow.
De novo assembly pieces reads by overlap; alignment parks them on a reference.
Gene prediction, ontology, transcript prediction and phylogenetics link sequence to function, increasingly with machine learning.
